report.headlineSummary: You’re not dealing with confirmed substance use, but you are seeing patterns that don’t sit right with you — inconsistency around rules, friction in conversations, and a home routine that doesn’t feel solid. That mix brings frustration and second‑guessing: “Am I overreacting?” and “If I don’t act now, does this get worse?” Both of those thoughts are normal at this stage. The work now is tightening boundaries and communication so you and your child are on the same team early, not waiting until there is a bigger problem.
report.topImmediatePriorities:
1. PARENT EMOTIONAL REGULATION  
- You’re worried about where this could go, even though you’re confident your child isn’t using and you’re not focused on safety risks like driving. That worry still shows up as sharp comments, impatience, or checking out. That’s normal with ongoing stress. Before any new conversation about rules, privileges, or behavior, pause and ground yourself — write down the two or three main points you want to say, step into another room for five minutes, and come back in calm. Your child needs to see steady, not frazzled.

2. CO-PARENT / CAREGIVER ALIGNMENT  
- You and your co-parent need to be on the same page about expectations, rewards, and consequences or your child will understandably test the gaps. Sit down privately and get specific: curfew, homework, phone use, chores, tone of voice, and what rewards and consequences are tied to each. Work out disagreements with your co-parent behind closed doors so your child sees one clear set of rules, rewards, and consequences instead of two different systems.

3. BUILD YOUR PERSONAL SUPPORT GROUP  
- BUILD YOUR PERSONAL SUPPORT GROUP — Join and actively post in the "Monitoring and Intervention discussion group." Connecting with other parents facing similar challenges can provide insight and support as you work through this. This group is an invaluable source of shared experience. Use it to sanity‑check your plan for rules, rewards, and consequences, and to hear how other parents hold the line without constant conflict.
report.keyPriorities:
1. BOUNDARY CONSISTENCY  
- Right now, rules are not enforced the same way every time, and sometimes privileges change depending on mood or how worn down you feel. That inconsistency teaches your child that pushing, arguing, or waiting you out might work.  
- With your co-parent, write a short list of 3–5 non‑negotiable rules (for example: homework before screens, tech off at a certain time, where your child needs to be and by when) and attach clear rewards and consequences to each. Keep it simple enough that both of you can actually follow through. The Auxiliary Workshop "Behavioral Contracts – A Tool for Positive Change" will walk you through how to put this into a written agreement your child signs, so it feels clear, not arbitrary.  
- Pair those rules with positive recognition — point out when your child meets expectations and follow through on agreed rewards. The Auxiliary Workshop "Setting Boundaries with Respect: Discipline Without Punishment" can help you enforce rules, rewards, and consequences without sliding into power struggles.  
- If you notice yourself backing off on rules or changing them mid‑week because you’re tired or the pushback is loud, the next step is to bring this specific issue to the "Monitoring and Intervention discussion group" and adjust your behavioral contract using the workshops above.

2. COMMUNICATION & CONFLICT  
- Conversations around rules or behavior may be getting tense fast — eye rolls, defensiveness, or you raising your voice more than you like. That wears you down and makes you dread bringing things up.  
- Shift the frame from “me vs you” to “all of us vs any choices that could hurt your future.” When you talk, lead with something like, “We care about where you’re heading and we’re seeing some patterns at home that don’t match that. Let’s figure out how we fix this together.” The Essential Workshop "Effective Communication: Building Trust and Engagement with Your Teen" will give you concrete tools to keep those talks from turning into the same argument every time.  
- During conflict, slow the tempo: if your child raises their voice, you lower yours. If you feel heat rising, say, “I’m getting too frustrated to be fair. I’m going to pause and we’ll finish this in 15 minutes.” Then step away — but keep the rules, rewards, and consequences you set; don’t drop them just to end the fight.  
- If most talks this week still end in defensiveness or shutdown, the next step is to schedule time to work through Essential Workshop "Effective Communication: Building Trust and Engagement with Your Teen" and bring one specific question from your hardest conversations to the "Monitoring and Intervention discussion group."

3. HOUSEHOLD STRUCTURE  
- Your home has some structure, but it’s not tight enough to support the boundaries you want — routines shift, expectations move, and that leaves a lot of room for arguments and loopholes.  
- Build a simple daily rhythm: consistent wake/sleep times, a clear window for homework, dinner, and downtime. Post a basic schedule where everyone can see it. The Auxiliary Workshop "Creating a Healthy Home Environment – The Power of Structure and Routine" gives practical examples of how to set this up without turning your house into a boot camp.  
- Connect that structure directly to your agreed rewards and consequences — for example, if homework and chores are done by a set time, your child earns a specific privilege; if not, that privilege is paused that day.  
- If the routine keeps slipping or you notice constant arguing over the same parts of the day (bedtime, screens, leaving the house), the next step is to revisit Auxiliary Workshop "Creating a Healthy Home Environment – The Power of Structure and Routine" and adjust one or two pieces of the daily schedule, then post how it goes in the "Monitoring and Intervention discussion group" for feedback.
report.whatToAvoid:
- Don’t launch into big talks about rules or worries right in the middle of feeling angry or drained — your child sees the frustration, not the care underneath it, and that usually leads to another fight.  
- Do not search your child's room, backpack, or phone in a confrontational way or as a threat in the middle of an argument; if you need to gather information, do it calmly, as a fact‑finding step, and follow the guidance in Auxiliary Workshop "How and When to Search a Room."  
- Don’t swing between no structure and harsh punishments — keep your focus on clear expectations, rewards, and consequences that you can enforce consistently.  
- Don’t turn every small issue into a lecture about “the future” — pick your moments, keep it short, and line up what you say with the specific behaviors you’re addressing.  
- Don’t handle all of this in isolation; skipping support from other parents and the existing ASAP structure usually leads to burnout and more inconsistency at home.
report.first72Hours:
DAY 1 — EMOTIONAL REGULATION + CO-PARENT ALIGNMENT  
- Before bringing anything up with your child, get yourself steady. Write down your top three concerns (for example: arguing over rules, ignoring chores, pushing limits) and what you want to be different in two weeks. This keeps you focused when emotions spike.  
- Meet with your co-parent (or another parent/guardian on the family side if you parent solo) without your child present. Agree on 3–5 core rules, the specific rewards, and the specific consequences attached to each so you both know exactly what you are holding.  
- Decide together what you will say the next time a rule is broken — one or two simple lines — so you are not improvising in the moment.  
- Make a clear agreement with your co-parent that, in front of your child, you will back each other up on those rules, rewards, and consequences and save disagreements for later.

DAY 2 — BUILD SUPPORT + GATHER INFORMATION + REVIEW RESOURCES  
- Join and post in the "Monitoring and Intervention discussion group." Share briefly what you and your co-parent agreed on and ask for examples of how other parents phrase rules, rewards, and consequences without constant fighting.  
- Before DAY 3's conversation with your child, review Auxiliary Workshop "Behavioral Contracts – A Tool for Positive Change" and the substance facts that match what you’re most concerned about in your community (alcohol, nicotine vapes, cannabis, fentanyl/opioids — medical risks, warning signs, and how use often starts). Having the information in your head means you respond from facts, not fear.  
- As a calm fact‑finding step, if secrecy or concerning behavior around belongings has already shown up, coordinate with your co-parent to check spaces where problems often show up (room, backpack, phone) using the complete search approach from Auxiliary Workshop "How and When to Search a Room": this is a fact‑finding mission, not a punishment, and must not be done while angry or emotional. Conduct any search of your child's room, backpack, or phone privately and without your child present. Leave the room as you found it and document anything relevant. If you find an unknown substance or paraphernalia, document it, confiscate it, and safely discard it — and treat that as a serious boundary issue, even though you are currently confident your child has not used.  
- Tighten one part of the household routine today — for example, set a firm tech‑off time or a consistent homework block — and tell your child clearly what the new expectation and related rewards and consequences will be.
report.days4to7:
- Stick to the rules, rewards, and consequences you set, even when it’s inconvenient. The goal this week is not perfection, it’s showing your child that you mean what you say and that calm, consistent follow‑through is the new normal.  
- Work through Essential Workshop "Effective Communication: Building Trust and Engagement with Your Teen" and Auxiliary Workshop "Creating a Healthy Home Environment – The Power of Structure and Routine." Pick one small communication shift and one small routine change to practice each day (for example, listening without interrupting once per day, or keeping a set dinner time).  
- Stay active in the "Monitoring and Intervention discussion group" — post an update at least twice this week on how your child is responding and where you feel stuck. Use the feedback to adjust your approach rather than starting from scratch each time something doesn’t land well.  
- If these patterns continue or intensify over the next week — ongoing intense conflict around rules, zero respect for agreed expectations, or early signs that substances are entering the picture — an ASAP-endorsed therapist becomes the right next step. For guidance, consider posting questions in the Sustaining Recovery discussion group. In Admin Spaces, under Treatment Providers, you can find a listing of treatment providers & therapists who endorse and support the ASAP program.
report.encouragement:
You’re stepping in before there is a confirmed crisis — that takes courage and it’s easy to doubt yourself when things aren’t “on fire” yet. This week is about you showing steady leadership at home, tightening structure, and making it clear that you and your child are on the same side against any choices that could harm their future, including substance use if it ever appears. Keep using the "Monitoring and Intervention discussion group" and the workshops named here; real change comes from steady, not flashy, steps.

Recovery is a journey—not a single event—and protecting the progress your child has already made is one of the most important responsibilities you have as a parent. While many adolescents go on to achieve lasting recovery, setbacks can occur. A setback does not erase the progress that has been made, and it does not have to become a return to the past.

Preparation is one of your greatest strengths. We encourage you to complete the Auxiliary Workshop "Protecting Recovery: Preventing Relapse and Responding to Setbacks." It will help you recognize early warning signs, respond calmly and effectively if challenges arise, and strengthen your family's plan to protect your child's recovery. We also encourage you to participate in the Protecting Recovery Discussion Group, where parents share experiences, encouragement, and practical insights while supporting one another through the ongoing journey of recovery.

Remember, the purpose of monitoring, supervision, conversations, and appropriate boundaries is not simply to discover what happened or when it happened—but to understand why. Identifying and addressing the underlying reasons for substance use gives your child the greatest opportunity for long-term recovery and a healthy, meaningful future.
